chapters.title: Justification and Righteousness
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible, being “righteous” is less about a perfect record and more about being set right with God and with others.
chapters.trueMeaning: Being in the right; set right; covenant faithfulness
chapters.nutshell: The Hebrew word family *tsadaq* describes being “in the right” within a relationship: keeping faith with God and with people. God’s own righteousness is His faithfulness in rescuing and setting things right. In Greek one word, *dikaiosynē*, means both “righteousness” and “justice”, and to be “justified” is to be declared and put in the right — welcomed into right covenant relationship with God.
chapters.bigIdea: To be justified is to be set right by a faithful God, and to be righteous is to live rightly with Him and with others.

In Hebrew, *tsadaq* means to be in the right within a relationship

*Tsedakah* came to mean giving to the poor — righteousness in action

To be justified is to be declared in the right and brought into God’s covenant family
Paul and James answer different questions and do not contradict each other
Justified people do justice

sections.h: Two English words, one Bible idea
p: When we hear the word **justification**, many of us picture a courtroom. We are guilty, God is the judge, and somehow the verdict comes out “not guilty”. When we hear **righteousness**, we often think of a perfect moral record, or of people who look down on others.

Those pictures are not completely wrong. The Bible does use the language of the law court. But English splits one Bible idea into two families of words: *righteous / righteousness* and *just / justice / justify*. In Hebrew and in Greek they are **one family of words**. If we want to hear what the first readers heard, we need to put them back together.

sections.h: The Hebrew words: tsadaq, tsedakah, tsaddiq
p: The root verb *tsadaq* (צָדַק) means **to be in the right**, to be justified in a case. A famous example is Genesis 38:26. Judah had wronged his daughter-in-law Tamar. When the truth comes out he says, “She is more righteous than I.” Tamar was not sinless; she was **in the right** in that relationship, and Judah was not. In the same way King Saul tells David, “You are more righteous than I” (1 Samuel 24:17).

The causative form *hitsdiq* (הִצְדִּיק) means **to declare someone in the right, to vindicate**. Judges are told to “justify the righteous and condemn the wicked” (Deuteronomy 25:1). Isaiah promises that God’s servant “shall make many to be accounted righteous” (Isaiah 53:11).

The nouns *tsedeq* and *tsedakah* (צְדָקָה) mean **righteousness**: doing what is right by the people you are bound to. Genesis 15:6 says Abraham trusted the LORD, “and He counted it to him as righteousness.” A *tsaddiq* (צַדִּיק) is a righteous person — and “the righteous shall live by his faith” (Habakkuk 2:4), where “faith” is *emunah*, steady faithfulness.

sections.h: Mishpat: justice that sets things right
p: Righteousness in the Hebrew Bible usually walks hand in hand with *mishpat* (מִשְׁפָּט), **justice**. God chose Abraham so that his family would keep “the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice” (Genesis 18:19). Amos cries, “Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24). Micah sums it up: “do justice, love kindness, and walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).

*Mishpat* is not mainly about punishing wrongdoers. It is about **setting things right**, especially for people with no power: the widow, the orphan, the stranger and the poor. A just judge in Israel defended the weak.
> When the Bible joins “righteousness and justice”, it is describing a whole community put right — not only one person’s clean record.

Here is something that surprises many readers. In the Psalms and Isaiah, God’s **righteousness** is often a word for His **saving action**. “The LORD has made known His salvation; He has revealed His righteousness in the sight of the nations” (Psalm 98:2). “I bring near My righteousness… and My salvation will not delay” (Isaiah 46:13).

In these verses God’s righteousness is not a cold standard that frightens us. It is **His faithfulness to His covenant promises**: He keeps His word, rescues His people and puts wrong things right. This is why a psalmist can say, “In Your righteousness deliver me!” (Psalm 31:1). He is not asking to be punished; he is asking God to be true to Himself and save.

sections.h: Tsedakah in Jewish life: righteousness you can give
p: In later Hebrew, *tsedakah* came to mean **giving to the poor**. To this day a Jewish charity box is called a *tsedakah* box. The idea is that helping the needy is not an optional extra kindness; it is simply **doing what is right**, because everything belongs to God and the poor have a rightful claim on His people.

Jesus seems to share this way of speaking. In Matthew 6:1 He warns, “Beware of practising your righteousness before others,” and the very next example is giving to the needy (Matthew 6:2). In the High Holy Day prayers, Jewish tradition teaches that **repentance, prayer and tsedakah** turn aside the severity of the decree. Righteousness is something you do with your hands and your money, not only a status you hold.

sections.h: The Greek words: dikaioō, dikaiosynē, dikaiōsis
p: The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, usually translates the *tsadaq* family with the Greek *dik-* family. *Dikaios* (δίκαιος) means **righteous or just**: Joseph is called “a just man” (Matthew 1:19). *Dikaiosynē* (δικαιοσύνη) means **both righteousness and justice** — one word. So “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5:6) could equally be heard as hunger for **justice**.

The verb *dikaioō* (δικαιόω) means **to justify: to declare in the right, vindicate, put right**. It does not always mean a sinner being acquitted. In Luke 7:29 the people “justified God” — they confessed that God was right. The tax collector in the Temple “went down to his house justified” (Luke 18:14) because he threw himself on God’s mercy.

Paul uses *dikaiōsis* (δικαίωσις), **justification**, in Romans 4:25: Jesus “was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.” Notice that the verdict is linked to the **resurrection**. When God raised Jesus, He declared Him in the right, and all who belong to Him share that vindication.

Paul writes that “a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28). James writes that “a person is justified by works and not by faith alone” (James 2:24). Both quote the same verse, Genesis 15:6 (Romans 4:3; James 2:23). Are they fighting?

Read in their Jewish setting, they answer **different questions**. Paul asks: who belongs to God’s covenant family? Is God the God of Jews only? (Romans 3:29–30). His answer is that Jews and Gentiles alike are welcomed by **trusting God**, not by first taking on the marks of Jewish identity. Many scholars think “works of the law” here especially means those boundary markers, though this is debated.

James asks a different question: what does real faith look like? His answer is that true trust always shows itself in **faithful action**, as it did when Abraham offered Isaac (James 2:21–22). Both men think like Jews: faith is *emunah* — trust that keeps faith. Paul stresses the **gift**; James stresses the **fruit**.

Many Western explanations treat justification **only** as a legal transaction in a heavenly court: a verdict changes, but nothing else need change. The courtroom picture is truly in the Bible (Deuteronomy 25:1). But in Hebrew thought the judge’s task is to **set things right**, and the verdict restores a person to their rightful place in the community.

So justification is about **relationship**: God, who is faithful to His promises, welcomes us into right covenant relationship with Himself and with His people. Righteousness then grows as a way of life — honesty, generosity, and justice for the weak. A justified people becomes a **just people**.
> “He has told you, O man, what is good… to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God.” (Micah 6:8)

chapters.title: Sanctification and Holiness
chapters.subtitle: To be holy is to belong to God — and it shows up at the dinner table, in business and in marriage.
chapters.trueMeaning: Set apart for God; belonging to Him
chapters.nutshell: The Hebrew root *qadash* means to be set apart: something holy belongs to God and is dedicated to His purpose. God sanctifies days, places, things and people, and His people then live out that holiness in ordinary life. In the New Testament *hagiazō* and *hagios* carry the same idea, which is why every believer is called a “saint”.
chapters.bigIdea: Holiness is belonging to God, given by Him and lived out together in everyday life.
skeleton: We often think holiness means being very serious or very perfect
The root *qadash* means set apart — belonging to God
God sanctified the Sabbath before He sanctified any place
Jewish life uses this word for blessings, wine, marriage and the honour of God’s name
In Greek, *hagiazō* and *hagios* carry the same meaning
“Saints” means all of God’s people, not a spiritual elite
God is the one who sanctifies, and we live it out in daily life

p: For many Christians, **holiness** sounds like a distant goal: being very serious, never laughing too loudly, keeping away from ordinary people and ordinary pleasures. **Sanctification** sounds like a long, lonely ladder of self-improvement that only a few “super-Christians” ever climb.

The Bible’s words paint a warmer and more practical picture. In Hebrew, holiness is first of all about **belonging**. A holy thing is not a strange or frightening thing; it is something that has been **set apart for God** and His purposes.

The root *qadash* (קָדַשׁ) means **to be set apart, to be holy**. Its active form *qiddesh* (קִדֵּשׁ) means **to consecrate, to make holy, to set apart**. The first thing in the Bible that God makes holy is not a mountain or a temple but a **day**: “God blessed the seventh day and made it holy” (Genesis 2:3).

Leviticus 10:10 teaches priests to distinguish between the **holy** and the **common**. “Common” (*chol*) does not mean evil; it means ordinary, not yet dedicated. A cooking pot is common; when it is dedicated to the Temple it becomes holy. Zechariah 14:20–21 looks forward to a day when even horses’ bells and every cooking pot in Jerusalem will be “holy to the LORD”.
The noun *kedushah* (קְדֻשָּׁה) means **holiness**. The adjective *qadosh* means **holy**, as in Isaiah 6:3: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts.”

sections.h: “I am the LORD who sanctifies you”
p: Leviticus 19:2 says, “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.” In Hebrew the “you” is **plural**: holiness is the calling of a whole people. And look at what Leviticus 19 goes on to describe: leaving part of the harvest for the poor, paying workers on time, not cursing the deaf or tripping the blind, being honest in court, and “you shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).

So biblical holiness is **very ordinary**. It is fields, wages, words and neighbours. Then Leviticus 20:7–8 holds two truths together: “Consecrate yourselves… I am the LORD who sanctifies you.” God makes His people holy, and His people respond by living as those who belong to Him.
> Holiness is not first something we achieve. It is something God gives — and then we live it out.

The same root runs all through Jewish practice. Many Jewish blessings begin, “Blessed are You, LORD our God, King of the universe, **who has sanctified us with His commandments**…” Lighting candles, washing hands, eating bread — ordinary acts become holy because they are done as service to God.

On Friday evening the family says the *Kiddush* (קִדּוּשׁ), “sanctification”, over a cup of wine to welcome the Sabbath; Jewish tradition connects this with “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exodus 20:8). In the synagogue the *Kedushah* is the part of the Amidah prayer where the congregation recites Isaiah’s “Holy, holy, holy.” The Kaddish prayer, also from this root, begins, “Magnified and sanctified be His great name.”

Even a Jewish wedding uses this word. Betrothal is called *kiddushin* (קִדּוּשִׁין), and the groom says to the bride, “Behold, you are **consecrated** to me.” She is set apart for one person. That is a beautiful picture of what holiness means: **belonging, faithfully, to one who loves you**.

sections.h: Kiddush HaShem: making God’s name holy
p: Leviticus 22:32 says, “You shall not profane My holy name, that I may be sanctified among the people of Israel.” From this, Jewish tradition speaks of *Kiddush HaShem* (קִדּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם), **sanctifying the Name**: living in such a way that people think better of God because of you. Its opposite is *Chillul HaShem* (חִלּוּל הַשֵּׁם), **profaning the Name**: behaving so that God’s reputation is dishonoured.

The Talmud (Yoma 86a) gives very down-to-earth examples: a person who studies God’s word but does not pay his bills or speaks rudely brings dishonour on God’s name; one who is honest and kind in his dealings makes people say, “Happy is the one who taught him!” Kiddush HaShem also came to mean faithfulness to God even unto death.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray, “Our Father in heaven, **hallowed be Your name**” (Matthew 6:9). “Hallowed” is the Greek *hagiasthētō* — “let it be sanctified”. It is the same longing.

sections.h: The Greek words: hagiazō, hagiasmos, hagios
p: The Septuagint translates the *qadash* family with the Greek *hagi-* family, and the New Testament keeps the Hebrew meaning. *Hagiazō* (ἁγιάζω) means **to sanctify, set apart for God**. Jesus prays, “Sanctify them in the truth; Your word is truth… for their sake I consecrate Myself” (John 17:17–19). Paul prays, “May the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely” (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

*Hagiasmos* (ἁγιασμός) is **sanctification, holiness as a way of life**. “This is the will of God, your sanctification” — and Paul immediately speaks about sexual faithfulness and treating one another honestly (1 Thessalonians 4:3–6). Hebrews 12:14 says to pursue peace with everyone and “the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.” *Hagiōsynē* (ἁγιωσύνη) is **holiness** as a quality, which believers bring “to completion in the fear of God” (2 Corinthians 7:1).
*Hagios* (ἅγιος) means **holy**, and *hoi hagioi*, “the holy ones”, is the word translated **saints**.

Paul writes “to all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints” (Romans 1:7). He even writes to the Corinthians — a church full of quarrels and problems — as “those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints” (1 Corinthians 1:2). In the New Testament, **“saints” means all of God’s people**, not a special few honoured after death.

Sanctification therefore has two sides, just like Leviticus. It is something **already given**: “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified” (1 Corinthians 6:11), and “we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10). It is also something we **grow into**, day by day, as God’s Spirit shapes us.

A common Western picture makes holiness private and inward, a matter of feelings or of keeping away from the world. The Jewish lens brings it back into the kitchen, the market and the family. Holiness is **belonging to God** and letting that show in how you speak, work, spend, eat, love and rest.

It is also **communal**. We are made holy together, as one people, and our shared life either sanctifies God’s name or dishonours it. Every honest receipt, every kept promise, every kindness to a stranger can be a small *Kiddush HaShem*.
> “May the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely.” (1 Thessalonians 5:23)

chapters.title: The Kingdom of God
chapters.subtitle: The “kingdom of heaven” is not mainly a place we go after we die — it is God’s reign coming to earth.
chapters.trueMeaning: God’s active reign, on earth as in heaven
chapters.nutshell: The Hebrew *malkhut* and the Greek *basileia* mean first of all **kingship** — God’s active rule — rather than a territory. “Kingdom of heaven” is a respectful Jewish way of saying “kingdom of God”, not a name for heaven as a place. Jesus announced that God’s reign was arriving on earth: already present in Him, and still to come in fullness.
chapters.bigIdea: The kingdom of God is God’s loving reign breaking into this world now and one day filling it completely.
skeleton: Many people hear “kingdom of heaven” as “heaven, where we go when we die”
*Malkhut* and *basileia* mean reign or kingship, more than territory
Israel was called to be “a kingdom of priests”
Daniel saw God giving the kingdom to the “son of man” and to His people
“Heaven” is a respectful way of saying “God”
Jews “take on the yoke of the kingdom” by reciting the Shema and pray for the kingdom daily
Jesus announced God’s reign: already here, not yet complete
The kingdom turns the world’s values upside down

p: Ask many Christians what the “kingdom of heaven” is, and they will say, “Heaven — the place where believers go after death.” On that reading, the gospel is mostly about **getting into heaven later**.

But when Jesus said, “The kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matthew 4:17), His Jewish hearers did not think He meant that heaven had come close. They heard something much bigger: **God is about to reign as King** — here, on this earth. To understand that, we need to listen to the Hebrew and Greek words.

sections.h: The Hebrew words: malkhut, mamlakhah, melekh
p: *Melekh* (מֶלֶךְ) means **king**, and the verb *malakh* means **to reign**. The Psalms shout, “The LORD reigns!” (Psalm 93:1) and “God is the King of all the earth” (Psalm 47:7). After crossing the sea, Israel sang, “The LORD will reign for ever and ever” (Exodus 15:18).

*Malkhut* (מַלְכוּת) means **kingship, reign, royal rule**. Its main idea is God’s **active ruling**, not a piece of land with borders. “They shall speak of the glory of Your kingdom… Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures throughout all generations” (Psalm 145:11–13). Notice how “kingdom” and “dominion” stand side by side.

*Mamlakhah* (מַמְלָכָה) is another word for **kingdom**. At Sinai God called Israel “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6) — a people through whom God’s rule would be shown to the world. Peter and Revelation apply these words to Jesus’ followers (1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6).

sections.h: Daniel’s vision: a kingdom that will never end
p: Parts of Daniel are written in Aramaic, where the word is *malku* (מַלְכוּ). Daniel sees the great empires of the world as wild beasts. Then “one like a son of man” comes to God, and “to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom… his kingdom is one that shall not be destroyed” (Daniel 7:13–14). Later the kingdom is given to “the people of the saints of the Most High” (Daniel 7:27).

This is the background of Jesus’ favourite title for Himself, “the Son of Man”. In Daniel, God’s kingdom does not rescue people **out of** the world; it **replaces the cruel empires** of the world with God’s own just and gentle rule (see also Daniel 2:44).

In Jewish teaching the phrase *malkhut shamayim* (מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם), “kingdom of heaven”, is common. Out of deep respect, Jews often avoided saying God’s name and used words like “Heaven” instead — much as we might say “the palace has announced” when we mean the king. (Compare the prodigal son: “I have sinned against heaven and before you”, Luke 15:21.)

This explains a puzzle in the Gospels. **Matthew**, writing for a Jewish audience, usually says “kingdom of heaven”. **Mark and Luke** say “kingdom of God” in the same sayings. Matthew has “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3); Luke has “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luke 6:20). **It is the same thing.**
> “Kingdom of heaven” does not mean “the kingdom located in heaven.” It means “the kingdom of the God of heaven” — His reign.

The Mishnah (Berakhot 2:2) explains that when a Jew recites the Shema — “Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one” — he first **takes upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of heaven**, and then the yoke of the commandments. Right after the first line of the Shema, Jewish tradition adds, “Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever.” Jesus’ invitation sounds familiar here: “Take My yoke upon you… for My yoke is easy” (Matthew 11:29–30).

The *Aleinu* prayer, said at the end of services, hopes for the day when the world will be **perfected under the kingship of the Almighty**, and ends with Zechariah 14:9: “The LORD will be king over all the earth.” The *Kaddish* prays, “May He establish His kingdom **in your lifetime and in your days**.” When Jesus taught, “Your kingdom come, Your will be done, **on earth as it is in heaven**” (Matthew 6:10), He stood right inside this Jewish hope.

sections.h: The Greek words: basileia, basileus, basileuō
p: The Greek *basileia* (βασιλεία) translates *malkhut* and likewise means **kingship, reign, royal power** as well as the realm ruled. In Luke 19:12 a nobleman travels to a far country “to receive for himself a kingdom” — that is, royal authority — and then return. *Basileus* (βασιλεύς) means **king**: the sign on the cross read “the King of the Jews” (Mark 15:26). *Basileuō* (βασιλεύω) means **to reign**: “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25).

Jesus began His preaching with, “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15). This echoes Isaiah 52:7, where the messenger brings **good news** and says to Zion, “Your God reigns.” The gospel is the announcement that God is becoming King.

Jesus said the kingdom had **already arrived** in His work: “If it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11:20). Healing, forgiveness and welcome for outsiders were signs of God’s reign breaking in. In Luke 17:21 He says the kingdom is *entos hymōn* — scholars debate whether this means “within you” or “in your midst”; many prefer “in your midst”, meaning present in Jesus Himself.

Yet the kingdom is also **still to come**. We still pray, “Your kingdom come.” Revelation looks forward to the day when “the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He shall reign for ever and ever” (Revelation 11:15). Like a mustard seed or yeast in dough (Matthew 13:31–33), it starts small and hidden and grows until it fills everything.

When Jesus says, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36), He is talking about where His kingship **comes from** and what it is like, not saying it has nothing to do with earth. His kingdom does not work like Rome’s. The poor, the mourners, the meek and the persecuted are blessed (Matthew 5:3–10). Children are the model citizens (Mark 10:14–15). The great are those who serve, because “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:42–45).

So the kingdom is not mainly about escaping this world but about **living under God’s rule within it** — forgiving debts, welcoming strangers, seeking justice and peace. “The kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17).
> Every time we choose God’s way over the world’s way, we pray with our lives: “Your kingdom come.”

words.note: God’s active royal rule more than a territory.
Israel was called “a kingdom of priests”.
The verb malakh means “to reign”: “The LORD reigns!” (Psalm 93:1).
The everlasting kingdom given to the “son of man” and to God’s people.
A rabbinic phrase; “heaven” is a respectful way of saying “God”.
Used for both “kingdom of God” and “kingdom of heaven”.
“King of the Jews”; “King of kings”.

diagrams.title: Two ways to hear “the kingdom of heaven”

left.label: Common Western assumption
items: A place we go after we die
Mainly about the future
Escaping this world
Mostly private and inward
Run like earthly power

right.label: Jewish lens
items: God’s reign, “on earth as in heaven”
Already here in Jesus, not yet complete
God putting this world right
A people living under God’s rule together
Upside-down: the servant is the greatest

events.d: Israel is called to show God’s rule to the nations (Exodus 19:6).
Isaiah and Daniel promise God’s coming reign over all the earth (Isaiah 52:7; Daniel 7:14).
Healings, forgiveness and welcome show God’s reign breaking in (Mark 1:15; Luke 11:20).
Jesus, “King of the Jews”, is raised and given all authority (Matthew 28:18).
God’s people live under His rule and pray, “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10).
“The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord” (Revelation 11:15).

verses.text: And you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures throughout all generations.
His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.
The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel.
Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

keyPoints: *Malkhut* and *basileia* mean God’s active reign more than a territory.
Israel was called to be “a kingdom of priests” (Exodus 19:6).
“Kingdom of heaven” (Matthew) and “kingdom of God” (Mark, Luke) are the same thing.
Reciting the Shema is “taking on the yoke of the kingdom of heaven” (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2).
Jesus’ prayer “Your kingdom come” stands inside Jewish prayers like the Kaddish and Aleinu.
The kingdom is already present in Jesus and not yet complete.
God’s kingdom turns the world’s values upside down.
reflect: If the kingdom is God’s reign “on earth as in heaven”, what part of your life most needs His rule today?
How does praying “Your kingdom come” change when you see it as a prayer for this world, not only the next?
Which of Jesus’ “upside-down” values is hardest for you to live out?

quiz.q: What is the main idea of the Hebrew word *malkhut*?
quiz.why: Malkhut means kingship and reign: God ruling, more than a territory with borders.

quiz.q: Why does Matthew say “kingdom of heaven” where Mark and Luke say “kingdom of God”?
options: “Heaven” was a respectful Jewish way of saying “God”
quiz.why: Out of reverence, Jews often said “Heaven” instead of God’s name. Both phrases mean God’s reign.

quiz.q: According to Mishnah Berakhot 2:2, reciting the Shema means taking upon yourself…
options: the yoke of the kingdom of heaven
quiz.why: The Shema is accepting God as King; then come the commandments. Compare Matthew 11:29–30.

quiz.q: Which prayer asks God to “establish His kingdom in your lifetime”?
quiz.why: The Kaddish prays for God’s name to be sanctified and His kingdom to come soon — very close to the Lord’s Prayer.

quiz.q: What does “already and not yet” mean for the kingdom?
options: It will only come after we die
It is present in Jesus now and will be complete in the future
quiz.why: Jesus showed God’s reign breaking in (Luke 11:20), and we still pray “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10).

terms.def: Kingship, reign, kingdom: God’s active rule.
Kingdom; Israel was called “a kingdom of priests” (Exodus 19:6).
“Kingdom of heaven”: a reverent Jewish way of saying “kingdom of God”.
Accepting God as King, especially by reciting the Shema (Mishnah Berakhot 2:2).
God’s kingdom is truly present in Jesus now, and will be complete when He returns.
